title: Job 2:7–13
context: Satan goes out from the LORD’s presence and strikes Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head. Job sits among the ashes and scrapes himself with a potsherd. Job’s wife says, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die.” Job answers, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” The narrator adds, “In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.” Then Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, having heard of the evil that has come on him, come by appointment to sympathize and to comfort him. Seeing him, they do not recognize him; they weep, tear their robes, sprinkle dust toward the sky, and sit with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without speaking, because his grief is very great. The sores should be told with pastoral restraint. The wife’s words should be reported as the text gives them, without vilifying her beyond the book; she has shared the losses, and the narrator does not pause to judge her soul. Job’s answer at 2:10 is the place to handle, fairly and in the regular notes, the same permission-and-decree difference already named at 1:12, 1:21, and 2:6, pointing again to Judges 9:23 and to 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, not to a new box. Shared ground remains: God is not the author of evil; Satan has acted only within the limit; Job is not charged with sin. The friends’ silence should be read fairly as sympathy and grief, not as the later speeches already begun. The speakers here are the narrator, Job’s wife, and Job; the three friends are named but do not yet speak. Both traditions close the prologue on unexplained suffering, a husband and wife in the ashes, and friends who sit still because the grief is great.

verses.text: So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says that Satan went out from the LORD’s presence “and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.” The second grant of 2:6 is now carried out, within the limit that Job’s life be spared. The sores are named and located, and they are not described beyond that. The speaker is the narrator; the agent who strikes is Satan, acting under the bound just set.

Arminian readers take the sores as a real affliction, permitted and limited, not authored by God as evil, and not a punishment the book has said Job earned.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep Satan as the one who strikes, under the LORD’s governing grant, without making God the author of the evil, and without charging Job with cause.

Both traditions tell the blow with restraint, and they rest on the shared ground already stated at 2:6.

verses.text: He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job “took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.” The narrator gives two details of his misery: a shard for the sores, and a seat in the ashes, a place of mourning. The verse is brief, and the comment is kept as brief and as sober as the line itself.

Arminian readers take the potsherd and the ashes as a real picture of Job’s condition, the servant of 2:3 now sitting in grief, still not charged with sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the scraping and the ashes as the narrator’s restrained account, Job himself in the dust, the integrity named in 2:3 not yet withdrawn.

Both traditions refuse to expand the sores or the ashes into a spectacle, and they invent no contrast over the posture.

verses.text: Then his wife said to him, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Then his wife said to him, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die.” The speaker is Job’s wife. Her words echo the LORD’s notice of Job’s integrity in 2:3 and the adversary’s hope that Job would renounce God. They are hard words, and Job will reject the speech. They should still be reported as the text gives them, without making her a villain beyond the book, and without turning the sentence into a theory of her motives. She has suffered the same losses of family and household; the narrator does not pause to judge her heart, and these pages do not do so for him.

Arminian readers take the question and the command as a real, bitter speech from a wife in the same grief, wrong as Job will say it is, but not an excuse to caricature her.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let her sentence stand in her mouth, a call to renounce God and die, which Job will refuse, without adding a condemnation the book itself has not pronounced on her.

Both traditions are fair to the verse: the words are sharp, they are not approved, and the wife is not turned into a stock enemy.

verses.text: But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job answers, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” The narrator adds, “In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.” The speaker of the question is Job; the closing verdict is the narrator’s. Job rebukes the speech, not by mocking his wife as a person, but by refusing words he calls foolish, and he includes her in the “we” who have received good. The word “evil” here is the calamity that has come, not a claim that God authors moral wickedness. Shared ground is again explicit: God is not the author of evil; Satan has acted only within the limit; Job is not charged with sin. The wording “didn’t sin with his lips” is the narrator’s in this verse, beside the broader “didn’t sin” of 1:22; no hidden inner sin is invented to fill the difference. As at 1:21, Arminian readers typically hear Job receiving calamity from God’s hand as from the God who permitted and limited it, with exhaustive foreknowledge, without God doing the evil. Reformed readers typically hear Job receiving calamity from the hand of the God who governs even this, in the terms of Judges 9:23 and of 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, while still denying that God is the author of sin. James 5:11 will later speak of the perseverance of Job and of the Lord’s compassion in the outcome; that later word may be named, but the outcome is not yet in view here, and it is not a new box.

Arminian readers therefore take Job’s question as faithful worship in the ashes, and the narrator’s verdict as a true acquittal of his speech.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same answer as Job’s confession that good and evil, as calamity, come at God’s hand, and they receive the narrator’s word that he did not sin with his lips.

Both traditions keep the existing box at Judges 9:23 in view rather than adding one, and they agree that Job is not charged with sin.

verses.text: Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite; and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator introduces Job’s three friends, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, who hear of “all this evil that had come on him”, and make an appointment “to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.” The speaker is the narrator. Their later speeches, beginning in the chapters that follow, are not the book’s endorsed doctrine, and 42:7 will later distinguish what the three have said from what is right. In this verse they have not yet spoken; their purpose is sympathy and comfort. The exact sites of Teman, Shuah, and Naamah are not settled here and should be hedged.

Arminian readers take the journey as a real, intended kindness, three friends coming together to sit with Job in his grief, before any argument has begun.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave this verse as an arrival for sympathy and comfort, and they refuse to read the later debate back into the appointment itself.

Both traditions name the three fairly at their coming, and they invent no contrast over places or motives the text has not yet tested.

verses.text: When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.
verses.arminianNotes:
When they lift up their eyes from a distance, they do not recognize him. They raise their voices and weep; each tears his robe and sprinkles dust on their heads toward the sky. The narrator describes a shock of grief: the sores have so changed Job that his friends, seeing him, do not know him, and they enter the same signs of mourning he used in 1:20. The verse is about recognition and lament, not yet about advice.

Arminian readers take the weeping and the torn robes as genuine distress at a friend’s condition, a fair beginning, not a pretense.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a real failure of recognition and a real mourning, dust toward the sky, the friends still in the role 2:11 gave them, to sympathize and to comfort.

Both traditions stay with the narrator’s picture and do not treat this lament as the first of the later speeches.

verses.text: So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” The friends’ first gift is silence, a week on the ground beside him, because the grief is very great. That silence is told as sympathy, not as already a failure of comfort. They will speak when chapter 3 has opened Job’s own cry; 42:7 will later judge the three friends’ words, not this sitting itself. The speaker is still the narrator, and the three have not yet opened their mouths.

Arminian readers take the seven days and nights as a real, costly staying with Job, a refusal to rush words into a grief they can see is very great.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let the silence stand as the narrator explains it: no one spoke, for they saw that his grief was very great. That is fairness to the friends at this point, not a verdict on the speeches still unsaid.

Both traditions close the prologue there, with Job uncharged with sin, the friends as yet unspoken, and no new keyContrast added over the heavenly scenes or the losses.
